nameStory: The name 'nannyberry' might come from this shrub's reputation as a reliable, nurturing presence in the landscape - like a nanny caring for children. Some say it refers to the berries being safe enough for a nanny to let kids eat them, while others think it's a corruption of an old folk name that's been lost to time.
description: Nannyberry is a tall, elegant shrub or small tree that can reach 15-20 feet high. It's one of our native viburnums, with a graceful, upright growth habit and glossy green leaves. In late spring, it produces showy clusters of creamy white flowers, followed by blue-black berries that birds absolutely love. The whole plant has a neat, well-groomed appearance that makes it popular in landscaping.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with finely toothed edges and a glossy, almost waxy feel. They're arranged in opposite pairs and turn yellow to reddish-purple in fall. The leaf stems often have a slight reddish tinge.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of tiny creamy white flowers in late May to early June, each cluster 3-5 inches across. The flowers have a sweet, pleasant fragrance that attracts bees and butterflies.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Berries start green, turn red, then ripen to blue-black in late summer. They're oval-shaped, about 1/2 inch long, and hang in drooping clusters. The berries are edible but quite tart.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that develops shallow furrows and scaly patches as it matures. Young stems are smooth and often have a reddish-brown color.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a large shrub or small single-trunked tree with an upright, somewhat vase-shaped form. Multiple stems often arise from the base, creating a clumping habit.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are long, narrow, and pointed, covered with reddish-brown scales. They're arranged opposite each other on the twigs and help identify the plant when leafless.

habitat: Nannyberry thrives in moist, rich soils along stream banks, forest edges, and woodland clearings throughout New England. You'll often find it in lowland areas, swamps, and the borders of wetlands, though it can tolerate drier upland sites once established. It grows well in both sun and partial shade, often forming thickets with other moisture-loving shrubs.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late April to May, followed by the showy white flower clusters in late May to early June when the sweet fragrance is most noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed with glossy green foliage, and green berries developing through July and August. This is when the plant looks most lush and full.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful shades of yellow, orange, and reddish-purple while the berries ripen to their final blue-black color. Fall color can be quite spectacular.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the plant's attractive form and the distinctive long, pointed buds. Some dried berry clusters may persist, providing winter bird food.

funFact: Nannyberry flowers are perfect little gender-benders - each tiny flower contains both male and female parts, but they're timed so the male parts mature first, then wither before the female parts are ready, forcing the plant to cross-pollinate with its neighbors like a botanical speed-dating system!
confusionNotes: Nannyberry is most easily confused with northern wild raisin, another native viburnum with similar berries. The key difference is in the leaves: nannyberry has glossy, finely-toothed leaves, while northern wild raisin has duller leaves with no teeth or just a few tiny ones near the tip. Remember: 'Nanny's neat teeth' versus 'raisin's rough edges.'
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - nannyberry isn't actually related to true berries like blueberries or strawberries. Its fruits are technically drupes (like cherries), with a single seed inside. The 'berry' in the name is just a common way people describe any small, round fruit.
compareHints: Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges. Northern wild raisin is similar but has untoothed or barely toothed leaves, while mapleleaf viburnum has distinctly three-lobed leaves like a maple. Hobblebush has much larger, heart-shaped leaves and a completely different sprawling growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
